The one-dimensional version of the data that preserves the most variance is the projection onto the first principal component.

[MATH: X^{T}X|= (UΣV^{T})^{T}(UΣV^{T}); = VΣ^{T}U^{T}UΣV^{T}; = VΣ^{T}ΣV^{T}.]

Since [MATH: \Sigma^T\Sigma] is diagonal with the squared singular values on the diagonal, the eigenvectors of [MATH: X^TX] are the columns of [MATH: V,] and the eigenvalues are the squared singular values. The largest eigenvalue corresponds to the first singular value [MATH: \sigma_1 = 2.075,] so the first principal component is [MATH: v_1,] the first column of [MATH: V{:}]

[MATH: [− 0.709; 0.706]]

To obtain the one-dimensional version of the data, we project [MATH: X] onto [MATH: v_1] by computing

[MATH: Xv_{1}|= [1.40|− 0.62; 0.01|0.43; − 0.85|1.19; − 0.56|− 1.00][− 0.709; 0.706]; = [− 1.43; 0.30; 1.44; − 0.31].]

Equivalently, we can compute this projection using [MATH: u_1 \sigma_1,] where [MATH: u_1] is the first column of [MATH: U.] Indeed, from the SVD,

[MATH: Xv_{1}|= UΣV^{T}v_{1} = UΣ[1; 0] = U[σ_{1}; 0; 0; 0] = u_{1}σ_{1}.]

Substituting [MATH: u_1] and [MATH: \sigma_1 = 2.075,] we get

[MATH: [− 0.689; 0.143; 0.695; − 0.149]]

which confirms the result.

Watch out! The vector [MATH: v_1] itself is the first principal component direction — a unit vector in feature space. It is not a one-dimensional representation of the data. The one-dimensional representation is [MATH: Xv_1] (or equivalently [MATH: u_1\sigma_1]), which is a [MATH: 4 \times 1] vector containing the projection of each data point onto this direction.

  4. Project the data. Compute the reduced data matrix [MATH: Z = X_{\text{std}} V_k,] where [MATH: V_k] consists of the first [MATH: k] columns of [MATH: V.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In previous lessons, we learned that the principal components of a standardized data matrix [MATH: X] are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, and that these eigenvectors appear as the columns of [MATH: V] in the singular value decomposition [MATH: X = U\Sigma V^T.] We also learned that the variance along each principal component is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value.

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to use principal components to perform feature extraction — the process of projecting high-dimensional data onto a lower-dimensional subspace while preserving as much variance as possible.

Content:
To illustrate the idea, suppose a biologist has recorded the resting heart rate and breathing rate for four mammals of different sizes. Both measurements have been standardized, giving the [MATH: 4 \times 2] data matrix

Content:
[MATH: [0.4|0.6; − 1.5|− 1.5; 0.4|0.3; 0.7|0.6]]

Content:
The biologist knows that body size strongly influences both heart rate and breathing rate — smaller animals tend to have faster rates for both. They want to extract a single "metabolic index" that captures this underlying factor. How should they proceed?

Content:
From the SVD [MATH: X = U\Sigma V^T,] the first principal component is

Content:
[MATH: [− 0.71; − 0.71]]

Content:
which points in the direction of maximum variance. To obtain a one-dimensional representation of the data, we project each row of [MATH: X] onto this direction by computing

Content:
[MATH: [0.4|0.6; − 1.5|− 1.5; 0.4|0.3; 0.7|0.6]]

Content:
The result is a [MATH: 4 \times 1] vector — one number per animal — that captures the variation in body size. The second animal, with the most negative standardized values (indicating a larger, slower-metabolizing animal), has the largest projected value.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: The Projection Formula

Content:
More generally, suppose we have a standardized [MATH: n \times p] data matrix [MATH: X,] where each row is a data point and each column is a feature. To reduce the data from [MATH: p] dimensions to [MATH: k] dimensions, we project the data onto the first [MATH: k] principal components. If [MATH: V_k] is the [MATH: p \times k] matrix whose columns are the first [MATH: k] principal components, the reduced data matrix is

Content:
[MATH: Z = X V_k.]

Content:
Each row of [MATH: Z] is a [MATH: k]-dimensional representation of the corresponding data point, expressed in terms of the principal component directions.

Content:
There is an equivalent way to compute [MATH: Z] using the SVD. Starting from [MATH: X = U\Sigma V^T,] we have

Content:
[MATH: Z|= XV_{k}; = UΣV^{T}V_{k}; = UΣ[I_{k}; 0]; = U[Σ_{k}; 0]; = U_{k}Σ_{k},]

Content:
where [MATH: U_k] is the [MATH: n \times k] matrix of the first [MATH: k] columns of [MATH: U,] and [MATH: \Sigma_k] is the [MATH: k \times k] diagonal matrix of the first [MATH: k] singular values.

Content:
So, we can compute the reduced data either as [MATH: XV_k] or as [MATH: U_k\Sigma_k.]

Content:
Watch out! The vector [MATH: v_1] (the first column of [MATH: V]) is a direction — a unit vector in feature space pointing along maximum variance. By contrast, the product [MATH: Xv_1] (equivalently, [MATH: u_1\sigma_1]) is the projected data — an [MATH: n \times 1] vector giving each data point's coordinate along that direction. Some texts refer to this projected data as "the first principal component of the data" or as "scores," so the term "principal component" can mean either the direction or the projected values, depending on context.

---

Item 3 — Example: Identifying the Best One Dimensional Reduction Given SVD of Data

[MATH: [1.40|− 0.62; 0.01|0.43; − 0.85|1.19; − 0.56|− 1.00]]
where the data has been standardized (the mean of each feature is [MATH: 0] and the standard deviation is [MATH: 1]).
We are also given the SVD decomposition [MATH: X = U \Sigma V^T] where:

[MATH: U|= [− 0.689|− 0.424|0.495|0.318; 0.143|− 0.241|− 0.524|0.804; 0.695|− 0.188|0.650|0.244; − 0.149|0.853|0.241|0.439]; Σ|= [2.075|0; 0|1.294; 0|0; 0|0]; V|= [− 0.709|− 0.706; 0.706|− 0.709]]

Explanation:
The one-dimensional version of the data that preserves the most variance is the projection onto the first principal component.

Recall that the principal components are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix [MATH: X^TX.] Using the SVD [MATH: X = U\Sigma V^T] and the orthogonality of [MATH: U,] we have

[MATH: X^{T}X|= (UΣV^{T})^{T}(UΣV^{T}); = VΣ^{T}U^{T}UΣV^{T}; = VΣ^{T}ΣV^{T}.]

Since [MATH: \Sigma^T\Sigma] is diagonal with the squared singular values on the diagonal, the eigenvectors of [MATH: X^TX] are the columns of [MATH: V,] and the eigenvalues are the squared singular values. The largest eigenvalue corresponds to the first singular value [MATH: \sigma_1 = 2.075,] so the first principal component is [MATH: v_1,] the first column of [MATH: V{:}]

[MATH: [− 0.709; 0.706]]

Equivalently, we can compute this projection using [MATH: u_1 \sigma_1,] where [MATH: u_1] is the first column of [MATH: U.] Indeed, from the SVD,

[MATH: Xv_{1}|= UΣV^{T}v_{1} = UΣ[1; 0] = U[σ_{1}; 0; 0; 0] = u_{1}σ_{1}.]

Substituting [MATH: u_1] and [MATH: \sigma_1 = 2.075,] we get

[MATH: [− 0.689; 0.143; 0.695; − 0.149]]

Item 10 — Tutorial: The Feature Extraction Pipeline

Content:
We can now summarize the complete pipeline for using PCA to extract features from a dataset.

Content:
1. Standardize the data. Subtract the mean of each feature and divide by its standard deviation. This ensures that all features contribute equally to the analysis, regardless of their original units or scales.
2. Compute the SVD. Find the singular value decomposition [MATH: X_{\text{std}} = U\Sigma V^T.] The columns of [MATH: V] are the principal components, and the diagonal entries of [MATH: \Sigma] are the singular values.
3. Choose the number of components. Using the singular values, compute the cumulative variance for each possible choice of [MATH: k] and select the smallest [MATH: k] that preserves at least [MATH: 90\%] of the variance.
4. Project the data. Compute the reduced data matrix [MATH: Z = X_{\text{std}} V_k,] where [MATH: V_k] consists of the first [MATH: k] columns of [MATH: V.]

Content:
To interpret results in terms of the original features or to apply the same transformation to new data, we must keep track of the means and standard deviations used in Step 1.
